Russian Occupation Update, May 29, 2026
Key Takeaways
Russia continues to pursue a policy of deporting Ukrainian prisoners, including female political detainees, to penal colonies in Russia.
The Russian government continues to fund University Shifts — a federal initiative that temporarily transfers Ukrainian teenagers to Russia to attend university classes with the goal of exposing youth to Russian values and forging long-term ties with the Russian state.
Russian social and ethnic affairs policy in occupied Ukraine continues to be solely premised on Russification and the eradication of any distinct Ukrainian identities.
The Zaporizhia Oblast occupation administration is preparing to further codify the supremacy of Russian language use in occupied Ukraine.
Russia is institutionalizing drone training programs in educational institutions in occupied Crimea.
The Mariupol occupation administration has reportedly launched a large-scale wave of evictions.
The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (MVD) has proposed measures to simplify the renunciation of Ukrainian citizenship in occupied areas.
The Crimea occupation administration is attempting to obscure its inability to address fuel shortages that are resulting from ongoing Ukrainian strikes against Russia’s fuel capacity.
The Russian government continues efforts to incentivize investment in occupied Ukraine.
Russia continues efforts to build up occupied Ukraine as an attractive tourist destination.
Deportation and Forcible Transfer of Ukrainian Citizens, Including Children
Russia continues to pursue a policy of deporting Ukrainian prisoners, including female political detainees, to penal colonies in Russia.
Occupied Crimea-based human rights monitoring group Crimean Tribunal reported on May 18, citing a source within the Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN), that Russia is transferring Crimean Tatar political prisoner Lera Dzhemilova to Penal Colony No. 28 in Volgograd Oblast.[1] Crimean Tribunal noted that Olga Chernyavskaya, a political prisoner from occupied Zaporizhia Oblast, is currently serving her sentence at Colony No. 28. The Crimea occupation Supreme Court sentenced Dzhemilova to 15 years in prison on treason charges in August 2025 on the allegation that she transferred information to Ukrainian intelligence.[2] Russia first began the practice of deporting political prisoners, often Crimean Tatars, from occupied Crimea to prisons deep within Russia following the annexation of Crimea in 2014, and has scaled up the practice since 2022.[3] The charges that Russia uses to justify the detention and deportation of political prisoners, especially Crimean Tatars, are fabricated or overblown treason, terrorism, or espionage charges. This policy likely violates human rights and humanitarian law, including the Fourth Geneva Convention’s prohibitions on the transfer of civilians from occupied territory.[4] Ukrainian General Prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko announced on May 21 that he submitted evidence to the International Criminal Court detailing Russia’s additional deportation of over 1,800 Ukrainian prisoners from occupied Kherson and Mykolaiv oblasts in November 2022 — emphasizing that the illegal deportation of prisoners is occurring beyond the context of Crimean political detainees.[5]
The Russian government continues to fund University Shifts — a federal initiative that temporarily transfers Ukrainian teenagers to Russia to attend university classes with the goal of exposing youth to Russian values and forging long-term ties with the Russian state.
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin signed an order on May 19 allocating over 155 million rubles ($2 million) to University Shifts for 2026.[6] The order states that the funding will provide for at least 2,300 schoolchildren from occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhia oblasts to attend Russia’s “leading pedagogical universities” across Russia, including in Samara, Tula, Volgograd, and Perm. Mishustin emphasized that University Shifts pays special attention to exposing teenagers to Russian “educational and cultural events.” Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered the creation of University Shifts in Summer 2022, and it has since facilitated the transfer of tens of thousands of Ukrainian teenagers to Russian universities for career guidance and cultural integration opportunities.[7] University Shifts also represents a Russian government-directed effort at long-term Russification, as it exposes Ukrainian youth to the Russian educational system and encourages them to forge long-term ties with Russia at the expense of their Ukrainian identities.
Sociocultural Control
Russian social and ethnic affairs policy in occupied Ukraine continues to be solely premised on Russification and the eradication of any distinct Ukrainian identities.
A conference on “the implementation of state national policy” took place in occupied Donetsk City on May 23 in accordance with the official designation of 2026 as “the Year of the Unity of the Peoples of Russia.”[8] Donetsk People’s Republic (DNR) Head Denis Pushilin addressed the conference at a plenary session framed around the claim that occupied Donbas is the “stronghold of [Russian] civic unity.” Several Russian milbloggers, including the prominent Rybar Kremlin-aligned media project, praised the conference and Pushilin’s speech, claiming that they emphasize the development of “Russian statehood” and Russian national identity in occupied Donetsk Oblast.[9] The conference comes six months after Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree in November 2025 officially approving Russia’s “State National Policy” strategy, which is aimed at “strengthening the unity of the multinational people of the Russian Federation, all Russian civic identity, civil unity and patriotism, [and] interethnic and religious harmony” in order to ensure Russia’s national interests and safeguard Russia’s national security.[10] The 2026 State National Policy, which will remain in force until 2036, codifies the Russification of occupied areas as a matter of Russian state policy.[11] The reflection of prominent milbloggers on the successful formation of “Russian national identity” in occupied Donetsk Oblast suggests that Russification measures are having tangible effects on identity formation and presentation in occupied areas.
The Zaporizhia Oblast occupation administration is preparing to further codify the supremacy of Russian language use in occupied Ukraine, likely at the expense of continued access to Ukrainian language sources.
Head of the ruling United Russia party’s occupied Zaporizhia Oblast Committee on Culture, Sports, Tourism, Ecology, and Youth Affairs Stepan Kuvachev announced on May 25 that the Zaporizhia Oblast occupation legislative assembly is drafting a law on the “protection of the Russian language.”[12] Kuvachev claimed that some businesses in occupied Zaporizhia Oblast are already replacing signs with Latin characters to Cyrillic characters, even before the law is passed. Russian occupation authorities and Russian federal law is already harshly restricting Ukrainian language use in occupied areas, particularly in schools, and the proposed draft law will likely contribute to even more intense efforts to privilege the Russian language in public spaces.[13]
Militarization of Occupied Areas
Russia is institutionalizing drone training programs in educational institutions in occupied Crimea.
Director of the occupied Simferopol-based Romanov Hospitality College Marina Palchuk announced on May 26 that the Romanov College and the Simferopol College of Radio Electronics received licenses to start “unmanned aerial vehicle operation” courses for the 2026/2027 school year.[14] Students of the Simferopol College of Radio Electronics previously received drone operation training from a Rosgvardia unit as part of the widescale “Drone Operator Cadre of Crimea” strategic project — an initiative of Crimea occupation head Sergei Aksyonov.[15] Chief Technical Training Specialist at the Crimean Research Institute of Unmanned Technologies Alexander Gritsenko additionally told Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti Krym on May 26 that over 2,000 students of technical and vocational colleges in occupied Crimea have taken part in the drone operator strategic project since February 2026.[16] The initiative selected 200 secondary-school students for further training, after which graduates can serve in the Russian military or various security agencies as certified drone operators. Aksyonov has previously claimed that “Crimea is the only region in [Russia] where a complete, end-to-end cycle” of drone operators has been established, starting with schoolchildren, refined in college and university students, and finalized in the “strategic talent pool.”[17] Drone training courses are now available for young children through the Artek International Children’s Center and primary school courses via the Fundamentals of Security and Protection of the Motherland curriculum, and the institutionalization of drone operation certificates at secondary education institutions further solidifies and streamlines the cycle of militarization.[18] The focus on drone training is especially salient as the Russian military grapples with recruitment challenges, including for its drone forces.[19]
Administrative and Bureaucratic Control
The Mariupol occupation administration has reportedly launched a large-scale wave of evictions in the city as part of longstanding efforts to seize and redistribute residential properties.
The Ukrainian Resistance Center reported on May 21 that the Mariupol occupation administration has started a widespread eviction campaign and that official eviction notices have begun appearing on the entrances of apartment buildings demanding that people leave their homes and surrender their keys to occupation authorities.[20] The Ukrainian Resistance Center posted pictures of some of the eviction notices and reported that authorities are also evicting residents who have gone through the “proper” steps of re-registering their properties under Russian law.[21] Mariupol occupation head Anton Koltsov notably announced on May 27 that his administration has begun a “mass” redistribution of previously abandoned housing from the municipal housing stock — the stock of housing transferred to the occupation administration via court order after being deemed “ownerless.”[22] While ISW has not observed evidence to independently corroborate Ukrainian reporting on the newest wave of evictions, ISW has previously reported on open-source evidence detailing similar patterns of evictions and property redistribution in occupied Mariupol and elsewhere in occupied Ukraine.[23] An ostensibly pro-Russian user of the VKontakte social media platform, for example, posted in August 2025 about evictions in occupied Mariupol and called the situation “dire.”[24] The Mariupol occupation administration is very likely using these forced evictions to transfer more housing to the municipal housing stock, after which it can be transferred to Russian immigrants in support of Russia’s broader campaign to repopulate occupied Ukraine.[25]
The Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs (MVD) has proposed measures to simplify the renunciation of Ukrainian citizenship in occupied areas, suggesting that Russian forced passportization measures in occupied areas may be encountering resistance.[26]
The MVD published a draft project in the Russian Federal Portal of Draft Regulatory Legal Acts on May 26 that proposes amendments to a 2023 MVD order on applying for “non-compliance with Ukrainian citizenship” by eliminating the requirement for an official Russian translation of documents. The amendment, if passed, would essentially remove the requirement to have Russian-language documents prepared for the formal process of renouncing one’s Ukrainian citizenship to obtain a Russian passport.[27] The removal of a bureaucratic barrier to entry for Russian citizenship suggests that Russian passportization efforts in occupied Ukraine may not be proceeding according to plan. Ukrainians living in occupied areas currently face a complicated bureaucratic process to obtain Russian passports, which are effectively required for anyone in occupied areas to maintain access to medical care and basic services.[28] Significant portions of the population in occupied areas may be resisting going through that bureaucratic process, however, and the Kremlin has recently issued simplified requirements likely in order to streamline coerced passportization processes.[29]
Occupation Administration Mismanagement and Internal Dynamics
The Crimea occupation administration is attempting to obscure its inability to address fuel shortages that are resulting from ongoing Ukrainian strikes against Russia’s fuel capacity in order to maintain the guise of effective governance.
Several Ukrainian and Russian opposition sources have recently reported that occupied Crimea has been facing intensified gasoline and diesel deficits in the last few weeks, and that the Sevastopol occupation administration has imposed a limit of 20 liters of fuel per vehicle in response to the shortages.[30] The fuel shortages are likely a direct result of recent Ukrainian mid and long-range strikes on Russian energy assets and fuel transportation logistics, but Russian occupation officials appear unable to adequately respond to the shortages.[31] Crimea occupation Minister of Fuel and Energy Vladimir Voronkin claimed on May 28 that the fuel shortages are a result of “technical issues” but that Crimea “generally has sufficient fuel reserves, so people should not panic.”[32] Voronkin’s dismissal of fuel shortages as a “technical issue” highlights the delicate balancing act that occupation administrations are engaged in. On one hand, the Crimea occupation administration is trying to posture itself as a legitimate and capable governing body, while also facing the mounting consequences of Russia’s illegal war on Ukraine. Official responses to fuel and water shortages in occupied areas have historically illuminated this governance dynamic.
Physical and Legal Repressions
Nothing significant to report.
Economic and Financial Control
The Russian government continues efforts to incentivize investment in occupied Ukraine.
The Russian State Duma passed a bill in its second and third readings on May 26 aimed at improving and streamlining the regulatory framework of the free economic zone (FEZ) that covers occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhia oblasts.[33] The draft law includes provisions that would reduce the minimum required capital investment from 30 percent to 10 percent, and authorizes the lease of land plots in occupied areas to participants of the FEZ without legal tender. The Kremlin established the FEZ in occupied Ukraine in 2023 and has offered participants reduced taxes and insurance rates for investing and operating in occupied areas, but the initial incentives were likely insufficient for the Kremlin’s intended vision for the FEZ given the Russian government’s subsequent efforts aimed at lowering barriers to entry even further.[34] The FEZ is more broadly intended to facilitate the economic integration of occupied Ukraine into Russia while providing Russia with a tangible way to profit off of its illegal occupation of Ukrainian territory. The FEZ also supports Russian efforts to attract Russian resettlement in occupied areas.[35]
Information Space Control
Nothing significant to report.
Infrastructure and Development Projects
Russia continues efforts to build up occupied Ukraine as an attractive tourist destination.
Russian Federation Council Senator from occupied Donetsk Oblast Alexander Voloshin told Kremlin newswire TASS on May 21 that Russia is developing occupied Mariupol to become one of the largest tourist centers on the Azov Sea coast “for decades to come.”[36] Voloshin claimed that in order to stimulate tourism in occupied Mariupol, Russia is investing heavily in the restoration of residential, transportation, and public infrastructure. The Russian Federal Unified Institute of Spatial Planning (EIPP) additionally told TASS on May 25 that it is forecasting that tourist flows to occupied Berdyansk, Zaporizhia Oblast, will increase to 1.5 million by 2044 due to the construction of new hotels and a yacht marina.[37] The development of tourist infrastructure in occupied Ukraine, particularly in areas along the Azov and Black Sea coasts, is a critical component of Russia’s campaign to forcibly integrate occupied areas into the Russian sphere of influence. Tourist flows to occupied areas normalize the occupation to both Russian and international audiences. These efforts ignore and obfuscate the fact that occupied Ukraine remains an active warzone, however, and that Ukrainian mid-range strikes are able to reach these occupied areas, which is likely to disincentivize active tourism as long as the war continues.

Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, May 28, 2026
Toplines
Russian President Vladimir Putin has likely developed a false perception of the Russian military’s successes in Ukraine based on heavily exaggerated maps from the Russian high military command.
A Ukrainian open-source cartographer and frequent geolocator published on X (formerly Twitter) on May 28 a reported leaked Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) map dated April 9 of the frontline in western Zaporizhia Oblast – the area of responsibility (AoR) of the Russian Dnepr Grouping of Forces.[1] ISW has reason to believe that the leaked Russian MoD map may be authentic. The map alleges that Russian forces seized Prymorske, Stepnohirsk, Richne, Veselyanka, Zaporozhets, Zapasne, Mali Shcherbaky, and Shcherbaky (all west of Orikhiv); southwestern Orikhiv up to the railway; and Novodanylivka, Mala Tokmachka, and Bilohiriya (all southeast of Orikhiv). Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov claimed on April 21 that Russian forces seized Veselyanka and entered Zaporozhets, and these claims are consistent with the leaked MoD map and show the Russian military command’s pattern of exaggerating advances in this area of the front.[2]
ISW had not observed evidence that Russian forces had infiltrated or advanced into Orikhiv, Richne, Veselyanka, Zaporozhets, or Zapasne as of April 9.[3] ISW observed evidence that Russian forces had entered (either through infiltrations or advances) but not seized Prymorske, Stepnohirsk, Mali Shcherbaky, Shcherbaky, Novodanylivka, Mala Tokmachka, and Bilohirya as of April 9. ISW has not observed evidence that Russian forces maintain a presence in Richne, Veselyanka, or Zapasne as of May 28. ISW has also observed no evidence that Russian forces have infiltrated or advanced into Orikhiv — the Russian operational objective in this direction since 2022. ISW observed Russian forces at closest infiltrating or advancing to positions about three kilometers from Orikhiv.
The Russian military command’s exaggerated claims about the Kupyansk area since late Summer 2025 show a larger pattern within the Russian military of misrepresenting the battlefield geometry at the highest levels.
Gerasimov and other senior Russian officials have repeatedly presented inaccurate situation reports about the Kupyansk direction. Gerasimov claimed in late August 2025 that Russian forces had seized approximately half of Kupyansk.[4] Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed in early October 2025 that Russian forces seized two-thirds of Kupyansk, and Gerasimov claimed in late October 2025 that Russian forces had surrounded 5,000 Ukrainian troops in Kupyansk and on the eastern (left) bank of the Oskil River east of the town.[5] Gerasimov subsequently claimed in late November 2025 that Russian forces had fully seized Kupyansk, and Putin claimed at that time that 3,500 Ukrainian troops remained trapped on the eastern bank of the Oskil River.[6] Gerasimov and Russian Western Grouping of Forces Commander Colonel General Sergei Kuzovlev claimed in December 2025 and January 2026 that Russian forces had seized Kucherivka (east of Kupyansk), Podoly (southeast of Kupyansk), Kurylivka (southeast of Kupyansk), and Kupyansk-Vuzlovyi (south of Kupyansk).[7] Gerasimov claimed on April 21 that Russian forces eliminated the purportedly surrounded Ukrainian troops on the eastern bank of the Oskil River, almost six months after Russian forces allegedly surrounded the troops.[8]
Russian milbloggers have repeatedly criticized the Kremlin and the Russian military command for lying about the battlefield situation in the Kupyansk area.[9] ISW observed evidence as of late December 2025 to assess that Ukrainian forces had largely liberated the town and were eliminating the remaining Russian infiltrators.[10] The Russian military command has nonetheless continued its exaggerated claims about Kupyansk in May 2026. Gerasimov claimed on May 16 that Russian forces were advancing toward Shevchenkove (approximately 28 kilometers west of Kupyansk), implying that Russian forces had seized Kupyansk and were advancing westward.[11]  Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov ordered on May 28 the Russian Western Grouping of Forces to increase the pace of advances in the grouping’s entire AoR — the Kupyansk, Borova, and Lyman directions.[12] Russian milbloggers have widely complained that inaccurate reports of Russian advances moving up the chain of command lead to senseless assaults that aim to capture the areas that the reports already alleged as seized.[13] Belousov’s order may aim for Russian forces near Kupyansk to increase their tempo of attacks in order to make the actual battlefield reality match that on the higher military command’s exaggerated maps.
The Russian military command’s exaggerations are likely leading Putin to believe his forces can achieve his battlefield goals in the near to medium term, despite the fact that Russia’s battlefield performance has steadily declined in 2026.
The
Financial Times
(FT) reported on May 28 that sources who talk to Putin stated that Putin believes Russian forces can capture all of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts by Fall 2026, after which he intends to escalate his territorial demands.[14] ISW assessed on May 13 that Russian forces have advanced at a rate of 2.63 square kilometers per day in Donetsk Oblast since the start of 2026, however, and that it is unclear when — if at all — Russian forces would be able to seize the rest of the region at this slow rate of advance.[15]
Russia’s rate of advance has significantly slowed so far in 2026 compared to 2025. ISW observed evidence to assess that Russian forces have advanced and seized 104 square kilometers in Ukraine between the start of 2026 and May 26 – compared with 1,619 square kilometers seized during the same time period in 2025. (These calculations do not include areas in which Russian forces may have infiltrated in 2026.) Russia’s net gains in 2026 are significantly lower than those in 2025 even when including areas in which Russian forces have infiltrated in 2026 but have not seized, which total 628 square kilometers. The Russian military command may be attempting to paint a better picture of Russian advances to conceal the true declining rate of advance. The Russian military command likely regularly shows such exaggerated maps to Putin, shaping his false perception of the frontline and the extent of Russian advances and likely leading him to make increasingly unrealistic demands.
Russian forces are reinforcing air defenses in Moscow City in response to Ukraine’s growing long-range drone campaign against the Russian deep rear.
A Russian insider source claimed on May 28 that sources in the Moscow City government confirmed that the Kremlin has shifted the burden of funding new air defenses, including those in Moscow City, to regional governments.[16] The source claimed that the Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) installed new air defense systems in Moscow City, but that the Moscow City government financed the project through contracts with Russian state defense conglomerate Almaz-Antey. Geolocated footage published on May 28 shows a Russian Mi-26 helicopter installing a Pantsir-SMD air defense system on the roof of the Nordstar Tower in Moscow City.[17] The system features up to 48 short-range TKB-1055 mini-missiles designed to intercept small drones.[18] Russian opposition source Vazhnye Istorii reported on May 28 that the Nordstar Tower is situated within three kilometers of the Sukhoi Design Bureau headquarters, the Moscow Garrison Military Court, the Russian General Staff’s Main Directorate (GRU) headquarters, and the Russian MoD’s 6th Central Research Institute.[19] Russian forces are reinforcing Moscow City air defenses following successful Ukrainian strikes on Moscow City and Moscow Oblast on May 16 to 17 and Russian restrictions in the Moscow air zone, demonstrating the increasing vulnerability of one of Russia’s densest air defense networks to Ukrainian long-range drone campaign.[20]
Russia continues to struggle to defend against Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign and is reportedly resorting to war crimes to protect Russian military vehicles in the rear.
A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed on May 28 that Ukrainian drone strikes against southern Ukraine are having far-reaching consequences on Russian logistics beyond just causing shortages of gasoline and goods in occupied Crimea.[21]  The milblogger added that Russia needs to find a way to protect its logistics but that Russian forces do not have enough personnel to erect anti-drone tunnels over their ground lines of communication (GLOCs) and machine gun nests. Another Russian milblogger added that Ukrainian mid-range strikes are targeting GLOCs 50 to 100 kilometers from the frontline that Russian forces use to redeploy forces and that these strikes could increase the successes of future Ukrainian counterattacks on the front.[22] The milblogger noted that roadside defenses are insufficient. The milblogger called on Russian forces to significantly increase the number of mobile fire teams and interceptor crews in southern Ukraine and to find ways to strike Ukrainian drone operators. Russian opposition source Astra reported on May 27 that Russian milbloggers are discussing an alleged order from the Russian military command to combat Ukrainian drone strikes in the operational rear by repainting and disguising military vehicles as civilian ones – an act of perfidy under the Geneva Convention.[23]
Sweden pledged a total of 36 Gripen fighter aircraft to Ukraine in a large military support package on May 28.
Sweden announced on May 28 that Ukraine will allocate 2.5 billion euros (about $2.9 billion) from the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan to procure up to 20 Gripen E/F fighter aircraft from Sweden and that Sweden will additionally donate 16 Gripen C/D aircraft to Ukraine.[24] Sweden also announced a military support package including unspecified long-range capabilities, ammunition, and electronic warfare (EW) capabilities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky noted that the Swedish aid package is worth $2.7 billion, of which almost $400 million will go towards drone production.[25] Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson stated that Sweden should deliver the 16 Gripen C/D fighter aircraft in early 2027 and aims to begin the delivery of the 20 Gripen E/F aircraft in 2030.[26] Kristersson stated that Ukraine has already started aircraft maintenance and pilot training.
Zelensky stated that the Gripens will help Ukraine defend against Russian guided glide bombs.
[27]
Zelensky stated that the Gripen’s Meteor air-to-air missiles with a range of 200 kilometers will help to displace Russian aircraft and hinder Russia’s ability to launch massive glide bomb strikes.[28] Russian forces have leveraged their sanctuary in Russian airspace where Ukrainian forces cannot intercept Russian aircraft in order to safely launch massive glide bomb strikes from a distance.[29] Ukrainian forces will likely use the Gripen fighter aircraft to deny Russian forces this sanctuary and force Russian aircraft further into the Russian rear, potentially far enough back that Russia’s glide bombs cannot strike frontline targets. Ukraine has also been building out its own glide bomb strike capabilities. Ukraine has developed its own domestically produced guided glide bomb, which will likely allow Ukrainian forces to expand their battlefield air interdiction (BAI) campaign against Russia’s near and operational rear, including against hardened targets.[30]
Key Takeaways
Russian President Vladimir Putin has likely developed a false perception of the Russian military’s successes in Ukraine based on heavily exaggerated maps from the Russian high military command.
The Russian military command’s exaggerated claims about the Kupyansk area since late Summer 2025 show a larger pattern within the Russian military of misrepresenting the battlefield geometry at the highest levels.
The Russian military command’s exaggerations are likely leading Putin to believe his forces can achieve his battlefield goals in the near to medium term, despite the fact that Russia’s battlefield performance has steadily declined in 2026.
Russian forces are reinforcing air defenses in Moscow City in response to Ukraine’s growing long-range drone campaign against the Russian deep rear.
Russia continues to struggle to defend against Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign and is reportedly resorting to war crimes to protect Russian military vehicles in the rear.
Sweden pledged a total of 36 Gripen fighter aircraft to Ukraine in a large military support package on May 28.
Zelensky stated that the Gripens will help Ukraine defend against Russian guided glide bombs.
Ukrainian forces recently advanced in northern in the Velykyi Burluk and Oleksandrivka directions. Russian forces recently advanced in Sumy Oblast.
Russian forces launched one Kinzhal aeroballistic missile and 147 long-range drones at Ukraine overnight.
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian Operations in the Russian Federation
The Ukrainian General Staff confirmed that Ukrainian forces conducted multiple Storm Shadow missile strikes on the night of May 26 to 27.
The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces used Storm Shadow missiles to strike hardware and software systems of the Russian Aerospace Forces’ (VKS) reconnaissance automation equipment near Voronezh City and Taganrog, Rostov Oblast.[31] Geolocated footage published on May 27 showed smoke and fires near the Taganrog Air Base and the Baltimore Air Base in Voronezh City.[32] The Ukrainian General Staff also confirmed that Ukrainian forces struck and observed a fire at the Tuapse Oil Refinery in Krasnodar Krai on the night of May 26 to 27.[33] The Ukrainian General Staff noted that the refinery has an annual refining capacity of about 12 million tons of oil.
Russian Supporting Effort: Northern Axis
Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border
Russian forces recently advanced and conducted infiltration missions in northern Sumy Oblast.
Geolocated footage published on May 16 and 28 shows Ukrainian forces striking Russian forces west of Popivka (southwest of Sumy City) and in northern Novodmytrivka (west of Popivka), indicating that Russian forces recently seized Popivka and Vysoke (just south of Popivka) and conducted an infiltration mission in northern Novodymytrivka.[34] Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets stated on May 28 that small Russian infantry groups have likely consolidated positions north of Taratutyne (southwest of Popivka) and south of Ryasne, and infiltrated in the northeastern part of Ryasne.[35]
Russian forces have not recently achieved tactically significant advances in the Sumy direction.[36]
Mashovets stated on May 28 that Ukrainian forces continue to control most of Ryasne. Mashovets stated that Russian infiltration missions from the Myropilske-Prokhudy line (west of Sumy City along the international border) toward Turya and Petrushivka (both south of Myropilske) have been unsuccessful. A Russian milblogger acknowledged that intense Ukrainian drone activity is hindering Russian advance near Zapsillya (northwest of Sumy City).[37]
Russian Main Effort: Eastern Ukraine
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #1
–
Kharkiv Oblast
Russian objective: Push Ukrainian forces back from the international border to create a defensible buffer zone with Belgorod Oblast and approach to within tube artillery range of Kharkiv City
Ukrainian forces recently advanced or maintained positions in northern Kharkiv Oblast as Russian forces continued infiltration missions in the area.
Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets stated that Russian forces have penetrated about 3.5 to 3.7 kilometers east of Vovchansk (northeast of Kharkiv City) along the line between Marino, Belgorod Oblast and Zybyne, Kharkiv Oblast but have not seized Zybyne.[38] Mashovets stated that Ukrainian forces likely continue to hold positions northwest of Zybyne and in southeastern Vovchansk. Mashovets stated that Ukrainian forces also continue to hold at least half of Vilcha (south of Vovchansk) and areas near Lyman and Prylipka (both southeast of Vovchansk). Mashovets stated that Ukrainian forces maintain control over Neskuchne and Zelene (both north of Kharkiv City) – areas in which Russian sources previously claimed Russian forces maintained positions.[39] Mashovets stated that small Russian infantry groups have been operating north of Symynivka (south of Lyman) and in northern Hrafske (southeast of Lyman) for one month (likely since late April 2026) but have not made additional gains since.[40] Mashovets stated that the Russian military command is equipping Russian forces in the Vovchansk direction with light motorized vehicles in order to increase advances.
Ukrainian forces likely maintain control over Hraniv (north of Kharkiv City).
Geolocated footage published on May 28 shows Ukrainian forces striking a Russian-occupied buildings in Hraniv and Shevchenka (north of Kharkiv City).[41] The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed on May 27 that Russian forces seized the settlement, but the Ukrainian 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Air Assault Forces refuted the Russian MoD’s claim on the same day.[42] The geolocated footage likely shows previous Russian infiltration attempts into Hraniv before the Ukrainian refutation.
Ukrainian counterattacks reportedly recently liberated Odradne (east of Velykyi Burluk) and nearby areas.
Mashovets stated on May 28 that Ukrainian forces liberated Odradne and advanced about three kilometers deep and about seven kilometers wide in the area after counterattacking in the Hryhorivka-Odradne direction.[43] Mashovets stated that Russian forces do not maintain stable control over Dvorichanske (south of Odradne). A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed on May 28 that Russian forces cleared Odradne after Ukrainian forces previously infiltrated into the settlement.[44]
The Russian MoD claimed on May 28 that elements of the Russian 69th Motorized Rifle Division (6th Combined Arms Army [CAA], Leningrad Military District [LMD]) seized Novovasylivka (southeast of Velykyi Burluk).[45]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #2 – Oskil River
Russian objective: Cross the Oskil River in Kharkiv Oblast and push westward into eastern Kharkiv Oblast and northern Donetsk Oblast
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Kupyansk direction on May 28 but did not advance.[46]
Ukrainian forces continue to interdict Russian frontline logistics in the Kupyansk direction.
A Russian milblogger claimed on May 28 that Russian forces will need to overcome Petro-Ivanivka (north of Kupyansk) to secure Russian ground lines of communications (GLOCs) on the western (right) bank of the Oskil River, implying that Ukrainian forces are successfully interdicting Russian logistics near the Oskil River.[47] A Ukrainian brigade operating in the Kupyansk direction reported May 28 that it discovered and destroyed a Russian UAZ-452 van, Zala drone, a motorcycle, generators, and manpower concentrations in the Kupyansk direction.[48]
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Borova direction on May 28 but did not advance.
[49]
Ukrainian forces continued their mid-range strike campaign against Russian military assets in occupied Luhansk Oblast.
The Ukrainian General Staff and Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) Commander Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi reported, and geolocated footage confirmed, that Ukrainian forces struck two Buk-M2 air defense system in occupied Kadiivka (roughly 50 kilometers from the frontline), a Nebo-SV radar in occupied Kamyanka (roughly 60 kilometers from the frontline), a logistics and support depot of the Russian 39th Separate Railways Brigade (Russian Railway Troops) in occupied Sorokyne (roughly 140 kilometers from the frontline), and a logistics depot and temporary deployment site of the Russian 330th Separate Radio-Technical Regiment (4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army) in occupied Tsvitni Pisky (roughly 95 kilometers from the frontline) on the night of May 26 to 27.[50] Geolocated footage posted May 27 shows damaged vehicles after a likely Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian artillery convoy along the Debaltseve-Luhansk M-30 highway near Debaltseve (roughly 50 kilometers from the frontline).[51] A Russian milblogger posted video May 28 of an overturned truck blocking the M-30 highway and claimed that aftermath of the strike blocked the path to Luhansk City.[52]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Donetsk Oblast
Russian objective: Capture the entirety of Donetsk Oblast, the claimed territory of Russia’s proxies in Donbas, and advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Slovyansk direction on May 28 as Ukrainian forces continued counterattacks in the area.[53]
Ukrainian broadcaster Suspilne reported on May 28 that the most intense fighting in the Slovyansk direction is near Riznykivka and Kalenyky (both east of Slovyansk).[54]
Russian and Ukrainian forces continue targeting each others’ ground lines of communication (GLOCS) in the Slovyansk direction.
The spokesperson of a Ukrainian brigade operating in the Lyman direction reported on May 28 that the Ukrainian brigade is targeting Russian GLOCs and drone operator positions, inhibiting Russian forces’ ability to supply forward infantry positions.[55] The Ukrainian spokesperson noted that Russian infantry sometimes emerge from their forward positions in search of food, allowing Ukrainian drones or infantry to eliminate the Russian infantry. The spokesperson noted that drone operators of the Russian Rubikon Center for Advanced Unmanned Systems continue efforts to interdict Ukrainian logistics. The commander of a Ukrainian drone unit operating in the Slovyansk direction reported on May 28 that Ukrainian drone operators are interdicting Russian GLOCs and striking Russian personnel shelters, fortifications, and weapons including artillery at distances up to 50 to 60 kilometers from the frontline.[56] A Russian milblogger claimed that Russian forces are interdicting the H-20 Slovyansk-Kostyantynivka highway, which connects the cities of Ukraine’s Fortress Belt.[57]
Russian forces continued infiltration missions within and near Kostyantynivka on May 28 but did not advance, as Russian and Ukrainian positions remain co-located within the city.
[58]
Geolocated footage published on May 28 shows Ukrainian forces striking Russian-held buildings in central Kostyantynivka after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[59] Geolocated footage published on May 26 indicates that Ukrainian forces retain positions in southern Kostyantynivka, contrary to Russian claims.[60] A Russian milblogger published claimed that Russian forces advanced in central Kostyantynivka seized Illinivka (south of Kostyantynivka).[61]
Russian forces continue offensive operations in the Dobropillya tactical area on May 28 but did not advance.[62]
Russian forces continue offensive operations in the Pokrovsk and Novopavlivka directions on May 28 but did not advance.[63]
Ukrainian forces recently advanced in the Oleksandrivka direction.
Geolocated footage published on May 28 shows Russian forces striking a Ukrainian position in Tovste (northeast of Oleksandrivka), indicating that Ukrainian forces recently advanced in the settlement.[64] A Russian milblogger published a map May 28 that acknowledges Ukrainian presence in Zelenyi Hai, Novokhatske, Andrivka-Klevtsove, Piddubne, Hrushivka, northwest of Filiya (all northeast of Oleksandrivka), and north of Oleksandrohrad (east of Oleksandrivka).[65] Russian milbloggers previously acknowledged a Ukrainian presence around and toward Piddubne on May 5, 8, 12, 13, and 26.[66] The Ukrainian General Staff reported fighting in Novokhatske on May 26 and May 27, further indicating that Russian forces do not control the Novokhatske and the cluster of settlements north of Piddubne.[67]
A Russian milblogger admitted that Ukrainian strikes are hindering Russian forces’ ground lines of communication (GLOCs).
A Kremlin-affiliated Russian milblogger claimed on May 28 that elements of the Russian Eastern Grouping of Forces are struggling to concentrate forces in their wide area of responsibility (AoR) in the Oleksandrivka direction due to Ukrainian strikes on Russian GLOCs.[68]
Ukrainian forces continue their mid-range strike campaign against Russian military assets in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF)  Commander Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi reported on May 27 that Ukrainian forces struck a semi-truck of a Russian S-350 air defense system near Kamyanuvate (about 120 kilometers from the frontline), a deployment point of the Russian 9th Motorized Rifle Brigade (51st Combined Arms Army [CAA], formerly 1st Donetsk People’s Republic Army Corps [DNR AC], Southern Military District [SMD]) near occupied Bezymenne (about 136 kilometers from the frontline on the Sea of Azov coast), and unspecified Russian logistics in occupied Donetsk Oblast.[69] Geolocated footage published on May 28 confirms the Bezymenne strike.[70] A Ukrainian USF brigade reported on May 28 that Russian forces had set up a military base at the Zirkona children’s camp in occupied Bezymenne.[71]
Russian Supporting Effort: Southern Axis
Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City
Russian forces continued infiltration missions northwest to southwest of Hulyaipole on May 28 but did not advance, as Ukrainian forces counterattacked.[72]
Geolocated footage published on May 26 shows a Russian soldier operating north of Pryluky (northwest of Hulyaipole) in what ISW assesses was an infiltration mission.[73]
A Ukrainian drone battalion officer operating in the Hulyaipole direction reported on May 28 that the Russian military command has deployed the most combat-effective elements of the Russian 5th Combined Arms Army (CAA, Eastern Military District [EMD]) to the Hulyaipole direction and regularly reinforces these units.[74]
Russian forces attacked northwest, west, and southeast of Orikhiv on May 28 but did not advance.[75]
The Ukrainian General Staff reported on May 28 that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian drone production facility in occupied Azovskyi Raion, Zaporizhia Oblast on the night of May 26 to 27.
[76]
Ukrainian forces continue interdicting Russian logistics and striking Russian fuel infrastructure at the near- and mid-ranges in occupied Zaporizhia Oblast.
Geolocated footage published on May 26 shows a destroyed Russian fuel truck near occupied Melitopol (about 76 kilometers from the frontline) on the M-14 Rostov Oblast-occupied Crimea highway after what was likely a Ukrainian drone strike.[77] Additional geolocated footage published on May 27 shows a Ukrainian drone striking a Russian vehicle on the M-18 Zaporizhzhia City-Mykhailivka highway north of Vasylivka (about 15 kilometers from the frontline).[78] Zaporizhia Oblast occupation official Vladimir Rogov claimed on May 28 that Ukrainian forces struck a gas station in occupied Velyka Bilozerka (about 28 kilometers from the frontline).[79]
Russian forces limited offensive operations southwest of Kherson City near Bilohrudyi Island on May 28 but did not advance.
[80]
Russian forces are committing personnel to escorting rear-area logistics to defend against Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign.
Kherson Oblast occupation governor Vladimir Saldo claimed on May 28 that engineer detachments of the Russian 58th CAA (Southern Military District [SMD]) clear Russian logistics routes daily and operate motorcycles and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) to provide cover for Russian logistics convoys, presumably in occupied Kherson Oblast.[81] Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign against occupied southern Ukraine, particularly against Russian GLOCs connecting Rostov Oblast and occupied Crimea, appears to be forcing Russian forces to commit personnel to counter-drone operations in rear areas rather than allocate the manpower to offensive operations.[82]
The Ukrainian General Staff confirmed on May 28 Ukraine’s May 26 to 27 Storm Shadow missile strike against Russian military assets near occupied Sevastopol.
[83]
The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck Russian Aerospace Forces (VKS) reconnaissance equipment near occupied Sevastopol.
Russian Air, Missile, and Drone Campaign
Russian Objective: Target Ukrainian military and civilian infrastructure in the rear and on the front line
Russian forces continued a series of long-range drone and missile strikes against Ukraine on the night of May 27 to 28.
The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched one Kinzhal aeroballistic missile from Lipetsk Oblast and 147 Shahed, Gerbera, Italmas, and other drones, including jet-powered Shaheds, from the directions of Oryol, Kursk, and Bryansk cities; Millerovo, Rostov Oblast; Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Krasnodar Krai; and occupied Hvardiiske and Cape Chauda, Crimea.[84] The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Ukrainian force downed 138 drones, that nine drones and the Kinzhal missile struck seven locations, and that debris fell on six locations. Ukrainian officials and Ukrainian media reported that Russian strikes damaged agricultural, residential, energy, and educational infrastructure in Chernihiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Poltava, and Odesa oblasts.[85] Ukrainian state energy operator Ukrenergo reported that Russian strikes caused power outages in Sumy, Kharkiv, Donetsk, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.[86]
Significant Activity in Belarus
Russian efforts to increase its military presence in Belarus and further integrate Belarus into Russian-favorable frameworks
Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign against Russia’s oil refineries is forcing Russia to import gasoline from Belarus.
Russian business newspaper
Kommersant
reported on May 28 that traders on the St. Petersburg Exchange purchased 17,340 tons of Belarusian gasoline from May 1 to May 22, up from 300 tons during the same period in 2025.[87]
Kommersant
reported that traders purchased 8,880 tons of Belarusian fuel from May 18 to May 22, almost four times higher than the previous week (May 11 to 15).
Kommersant
reported that the Russian market is experiencing a supply shortage of gasoline due to claimed” seasonal and unscheduled refinery repairs.” Ukrainian forces have significantly increased the frequency, range, and intensity of strikes against Russian oil infrastructure since March 2026.[88]
Kommersant
noted that Russian buyers are increasingly turning to Belarusian fuel despite higher prices, demonstrating close cooperation between the Russian and Belarusian economies as Belarusian refineries provide Russian buyers with relatively stable gasoline supplies to compensate for Russian shortages and market instability.[89]
Russia and Belarus are continuing government integration efforts by coordinating statistical standards.
The press service of the National Statistical Committee of the Republic of Belarus (Belstat) reported on May 28 that Belstat and the Russian Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat) signed a plan to coordinate statistical methodology from 2027 until 2029.[90]

Iran Update Special Report, May 28, 2026
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and
The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute
are publishing daily updates to provide analysis on the war with Iran. The updates focus on US and Israeli strikes on Iran and Iran and the Axis of Resistance’s response to the strikes. The updates cover events from the past 24-hour period.
Key Takeaways
Western media reported on May 28 that US and Iranian negotiators have reached a 60-day memorandum of understanding (MoU), but the US and Iranian leaders who must approve the agreement—US President Donald Trump and Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, respectively—have not approved the “agreement” at this time. The details of the reported “agreement” are also unclear based on the wording and sourcing of the leaks of the agreement.
Even if Iranian negotiators did offer some concessions, it is far from clear that senior decision-makers in Tehran, including Mojtaba Khamenei and IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi, are willing to make such concessions. Mojtaba Khamenei’s recent public statements indicate that he is not willing to give up Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC is using force to try to create the reality that Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz. US Central Command’s (CENTCOM) recent military strikes against Iran are part of an effort to deny Iran the ability to create that reality.
The United States is taking steps to prevent Iranian efforts to establish a protection racket in the Strait of Hormuz. The US Treasury Department sanctioned the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) on May 27 and warned that any actor that cooperates with the PGSA could face sanctions.
Toplines
Western media reported on May 28 that US and Iranian negotiators have reached a 60-day memorandum of understanding (MoU), but the US and Iranian leaders who must approve the agreement—US President Donald Trump and Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, respectively—have not approved the “agreement” at this time. The details of the reported “agreement” are also unclear based on the wording and sourcing of the leaks of the agreement.[1]
Two unspecified US officials told Axios on May 28 that US and Iranian negotiators have reached a 60-day MoU to extend the ceasefire and launch negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program.[2] The officials claimed that Iranian negotiators received the “necessary approvals” from “senior leadership” to sign the deal. Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC)-affiliated Tasnim News Agency, citing a source close to the negotiating team, denied that an MoU has been “finalized,” however.[3] An unspecified source also told Israeli media that Mojtaba has not yet approved the “agreement.”[4]
The US officials told Axios that Iran would allow “unrestricted” shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, stop imposing tolls and harassing vessels in the strait, and remove naval mines within 30 days, while the United States would lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports.[5] The officials did not specify how the MoU defines “unrestricted” shipping. Iranian officials have repeatedly described the strait as “open” to shipping while forcing vessels to receive Iranian permission to pass through the strait and to use Iran’s illegal traffic separation scheme.[6] Iranian officials have also claimed that Iran is charging vessels “protection fees” and “environmental fees” instead of “tolls.”[7] The ambiguity around these terms makes it unclear whether Iranian negotiators have actually committed to any concessions in the reported MoU.
Even if Iranian negotiators did offer some concessions, it is far from clear that senior decision-makers in Tehran, including Mojtaba
Khamenei
and IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi, are willing to make such concessions.
Mojtaba’s recent public statements indicate that he is not willing to give up Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz.[8] IRGC-affiliated media has also insisted that Iran must receive economic relief—including the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets—before Iran will discuss its nuclear program.[9] ISW-CTP continues to assess that Vahidi and his inner circle are currently dominating Iranian decision-making. The US officials told Axios that the United States would discuss sanctions relief and the release of Iran’s frozen assets during the 60-day negotiations period, in contrast to the Iranian regime’s demand for immediate economic relief upon the signing of an agreement. If Iranian negotiators did agree to postpone the discussion of economic relief to the 60-day negotiations period, this would indicate that Iranian negotiators may not be aligned with Mojtaba and Vahidi. Anti-regime media, citing a source close to the negotiations, reported on May 28 that there are doubts among unspecified individuals about Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and the negotiating team’s coordination with Mojtaba, which further suggests that the terms in the reported US-Iran MoU may not reflect the positions of key Iranian leaders in Tehran.[10]
The IRGC is using force to try to create the reality that Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz. US Central Command’s (CENTCOM) recent military strikes against Iran are part of an effort to deny Iran the ability to create such a reality.
Iranian state media claimed on May 28 that the IRGC Navy issued a “stern warning” to four vessels that attempted to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without Iranian permission.[11] The report claimed that the IRGC Navy seized two of the vessels and forced the other two vessels to turn around.[12] US CENTCOM reported on May 28 that US forces intercepted five Iranian one-way attack drones that threatened US forces and commercial shipping in the strait.[13] CENTCOM added that US forces struck an Iranian drone launch site in Bandar Abbas, Hormozgan Province, that was preparing to launch a sixth drone.[14] It is possible that the Iranian drones were targeting the vessels that Iranian media claimed attempted to transit through the strait without coordinating with Iran. Iran has repeatedly used force, including attacks on commercial vessels and naval mines, to force vessels to transit through its illegal traffic separation scheme and comply with Iranian transit regulations. US forces recently struck two IRGC Navy mine-laying vessels on May 25. Iran responded to the US strikes by launching a ballistic missile at an unspecified US airbase in Kuwait, but Kuwaiti air defenses intercepted the missile.
ISW-CTP is tracking initial IRGC-affiliated media reporting of Iranian missile attacks launched from southern Iran targeting US naval vessels in an unspecified location in the Persian Gulf as of 3:58 PM ET on May 28.[15] ISW-CTP will provide further analysis about these reports on May 29.
The United States is taking steps to prevent Iranian efforts to establish a protection racket in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US Treasury Department sanctioned the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) on May 27 and warned that any actor that cooperates with the PGSA could face sanctions.[16] The PGSA is an organization that Iran established to formalize its control over the strait and force commercial vessels to pay tolls and coordinate their movements with Iran.[17] US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also threatened to economically target any actors, including Oman, that directly or indirectly facilitate tolls in the strait.[18] Bessent’s comments follow multiple reports that Iran has discussed establishing a system with Oman to jointly collect tolls from vessels that transit through the strait.[19]
US-Iran Negotiations
See topline section.
Maritime Activity in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf
See topline section.
US and Israeli Air Campaign
See topline section.
Regime Dynamics in Iran
The Iranian Parliament re-elected Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as parliament speaker for his seventh consecutive term in the Iranian Parliament’s annual presidium election on May 25.[20]
It is very rare, if not unprecedented, for parliamentarians to oust the incumbent parliament speaker during the annual presidium election, and it would have therefore been noteworthy if parliamentarians had voted to remove Ghalibaf.
Ghalibaf’s removal would have been particularly notable given the role he has played in leading Iran’s negotiating delegation in recent months.
Ghalibaf won 235 votes from the 285 parliamentarians who voted. The other two candidates for parliament speaker were ultraconservative Paydari (Stability) Front candidate Mohammad Taghi Naghdali and Sunni candidate Osman Salari, who received 29 and seven votes, respectively.[21] Parliament also re-elected Ali Nikzad and Hamid Reza Haji Babaei as deputy parliament speakers.[22] Ghalibaf has served as parliament speaker since 2020, before which Ali Larijani held the position for 12 years
.
[23]
Iran’s Axis of Resistance
Lebanese Hezbollah and the Israeli Campaign in Lebanon
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) conducted a strike in Beirut’s vicinity for the first time since May 6, after the IDF reportedly received US approval to target Hezbollah-affiliated commanders in the area.
[24] The IDF announced that it conducted a strike in Beirut on May 28.[25] Israeli media and open-source intelligence (OSINT) accounts reported that the strike targeted Imam Hussein Division Missile Force Commander Ali al Husseini in Chouaifet, Aley District, which is located in Beirut’s metropolitan area.[26] The IDF has not confirmed that its strike targeted Husseini at the time of this writing, however. The IRGC Quds Force uses the Imam Hussein Division to conduct attacks against the IDF and Israel.[27] The IDF struck and killed former Imam Hussein Division Commander Hassan Ali Marwan in Beirut on March 17.[28] The IDF strike in Chouaifet marks the first IDF strike in Beirut’s vicinity since the IDF killed Hezbollah Radwan Force Commander Ahmad Ghaleb “Malik” Balout in Beirut’s southern suburbs on May 6.[29] The IDF’s strike follows recent reports that US officials support allowing the IDF to target Hezbollah commanders in Beirut.[30] A senior Israeli official told Israeli media on May 26 that the United States told Israel not to conduct large attacks in Beirut but authorized Israel to conduct targeted strikes against Hezbollah commanders.[31]
The IDF has expanded its ground and air campaigns in Lebanon in recent days and has made limited advances beyond the “Yellow Line.”[32]
The IDF confirmed on May 28 that it has conducted “raids” beyond the “Yellow Line” to push Hezbollah fighters deeper into Lebanon and protect Israeli forces in southern Lebanon and northern Israel from Hezbollah first-person view (FPV) drone attacks.[33]  Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on May 26 that the IDF will seize “strategic positions” during expanded ground operations and confirmed on May 28 that Israeli forces have advanced north of the Litani River.[34] An OSINT analyst posted satellite imagery on May 28 showing several IDF tanks positioned north of the Litani River in Yohmor, Nabatieh District.[35] The analyst previously posted imagery on May 26 showing IDF tanks in nearby Zawtar al Charqiyeh, Nabatieh District, which was the IDF’s bridgehead for ground operations north of the Litani.[36] Hezbollah claimed on May 27 that it used direct fire on Israeli forces in Zawtar al Charqiyeh, which Hezbollah has typically avoided except for the group’s recent attempts to defend against Israeli ground advances.[37] The IDF has also expanded its air campaign in Lebanon and claimed that it has struck nearly 700 Hezbollah targets since May 24.[38] The IDF struck at least six Hezbollah sites in the northern Beqaa Valley, in addition to striking around 15 targets in the vicinity of Tyre on May 27 and 28.[39] The IDF also issued an order on May 27 for civilians to evacuate all Lebanese territory south of the Zahrani River for the first time and declared all territory south of the river a ”combat zone.”[40]
Other Axis of Resistance Activity
Nothing significant to report.
